sections.body:
Is good a quality that one person has and bad a quality that another person has, or are the two ways of using the same capacity? The working answer of this article is the second one. The capacity — the ability to read a face, to judge a situation, to make a room follow you — belongs to one person. The good and the bad are two aims given to that one capacity.

Every act has five parts, and it pays to name them. The **capacity** is what you can do. The **motive** is the aim behind the act: what you are doing it for. The **means** is how the aim is carried out: the tools, the words, the methods. The **habit** is the act repeated until it needs no thought. The **character** is what a person does as a rule, when nobody is checking. The first three describe one act. The last two describe what a series of acts adds up to.

In this article, **evil** means harm done on purpose. It does not mean a religion, a spirit, or a permanent label on a person. The subject is the mechanism of a decision, not a doctrine about the universe. Researchers disagree about how much of a decision is made quickly and how much slowly, and about how much a person can control either part. Nothing here depends on that argument: whatever the split, a decision has an aim, a habit and a moment, and the moment can be moved.

There is one limit to say at the start. A mechanism explains why a decision happened. It does not say the decision was right, and it does not move the responsibility away from the person who made it.
examples: The capacity was there; the aim decided what it was used for.
His motive was to keep the machine running, and the motive decided the rest.
It was a habit, and the habit had been built one small repetition at a time.
sections.heading: Good and bad: one capacity, two aims

terms.example: He had the capacity to read a face well, and the capacity was never the question.
terms.gloss: The ability you have to do something, whatever you decide to do it for.

terms.example: The motive was to keep the machine running, and the motive decided the rest.
terms.gloss: The aim that is behind an act: what the act is for.

terms.example: The means were ordinary tools used in an ordinary way.
terms.gloss: The way an aim is carried out: the tools, the words and the methods used.

terms.example: It was a habit, and the habit had been built one small repetition at a time.
terms.gloss: An act repeated until it can be done without thinking about it.

terms.example: Character is what you do when nobody is checking.
terms.gloss: What a person does as a rule, when nobody is checking.

sections.body:
The capacity to say what you want, to judge a situation, to convince other people and to act is one capacity. It does not come in two versions. A surgeon and a scammer both read a face well. A team leader and a bully both know how to make a room follow. The skill is the same on both sides of the sentence.

The tool is neutral; the aim is not. A knife cuts rope and cuts a throat. What makes an act good or bad is not the sharpness of the tool but the **motive** behind it and the **means** it uses. When you look at a decision, ask two questions: what was it for, and what did it do to the other side? Those two questions tell you more than any list of traits.

This is why *a good person* is a poor question. A **capacity** is not a verdict, and a verdict tells you nothing about the next decision. The useful question is what a person is doing with the capacity today, under which aim, with which audience present, at which hour of the day.
examples: He had the skill; the aim decided whether it helped or harmed.
Same tool, different aim: the difference is in what it was for.
Ask what it was for, and who carried the cost.
sections.heading: The same tool, two uses

sections.body:
Every mind holds two sets of arguments about the same act. One set supports it and the other stops it. The second set is not a weakness and the first set is not a virtue. They are the two sides of one decision, and most of the time both are present at the same time.

The pause between them is short. For many people it is shortest at the end of a long shift, late at night, or after a bad hour, and longest in the morning when nothing is pressing. That space is the work of **deliberation**: one argument put against the other before you act. The space is not empty. It is short.

The argument that harms is often the faster one, and the reason is plain. It is the older **habit**, so its wording is already ready. It speaks in the language of the moment: the deadline, the crowd, the money. The other argument has to be built each time, and a **counter-argument** assembled from nothing loses to a habit that has been rehearsed for years.

An **impulse** makes the gap smaller. An impulse is a push to act before you have thought, and it arrives with its own justification attached. This is why one person can be generous on Monday and cruel on Friday: the same capacity, the same person, different conditions around the decision.
examples: Both arguments were there, and the older one answered first.
I am tired, and the tired argument is the one that arrives ready-made.
There is a counter-argument here, and I have to say it out loud before I decide.
sections.heading: Two arguments inside the same person

terms.example: Deliberation took two minutes, and the two minutes were enough.
terms.gloss: The short space in which one argument is weighed against another.

terms.example: The counter-argument was short, and it changed the decision.
terms.gloss: The argument made against a decision that is still being considered.

terms.example: The impulse to reply at once was stronger than the answer.
terms.gloss: A sudden push to act before you have thought it through.

sections.body:
The capacity is fixed. Six things around the decision decide what it produces, and they can be checked one at a time.

Two of them belong to the decision itself. The **aim** says what the act is for. The **habit** says what the person does without thinking, because the check is the first thing a hurried or tired person drops. The **temptation** is the pull of a gain that somebody else pays for; it is strongest when the gain arrives now and the cost arrives later, which is the usual shape of a decision at work.

Two of them belong to the people. The **audience** is who is present and watching. An act performed for an audience takes the shape the audience wants, and the audience changes the act even when nobody says a word. The **time and the tiredness** narrow what a person notices: at the end of a long shift a request can read as a demand and a delay as an insult.

The last one is the **moment of decision** — whether the act is made in the open, where somebody can question it, or alone at the end of the day, where nobody will.
examples: The aim was the number, and the person was only a way to reach it.
With the customer in the room, the audience changed what he said.
The decision was made alone, at the end of the day, where nobody would question it.
sections.heading: What turns the same capacity into help or into harm

rows: The aim is what the act is done for.
The aim is to keep the machine running and the people safe, so the capacity is used for its purpose.
The aim is to win the quarter, and the person is only a means to the number.
The people who are there are the people who see the act.
The people present can see what the act does to other people, and they can stop it.
The people present want the result and do not want to look at the cost.
The time and the tiredness are how late the decision is and how tired the person is.
The decision is taken early, with time to check the facts and to ask somebody else.
The decision is taken at the end of a long shift, when attention is narrow and the answer has to be quick.
The habit is what the person does without thinking about it.
The habit is to check, so the check happens without anybody asking for it.
The habit is to protect your own position, so the check is the first thing to be dropped.
The audience is the people who watch the act.
The audience is the people who will live with the result, and it pulls the decision towards their interest.
The audience is the people who will be rewarded for the result, and it pulls the decision away from the cost.
The moment of decision is when and where the act is made.
The decision is made in the open, where somebody else can question it.
The decision is made alone, at the end of the day, where nobody will question it.

terms.example: The temptation was the extra 200 $ that the supplier would pay for.
terms.gloss: The pull of a gain that somebody else pays the cost of.

terms.example: With the customer in the room, the audience changed what he said.
terms.gloss: The people who are present and watching when you act.

sections.body:
Six steps. They take a few minutes, they need no tool, and they work the same at work, at home and in a meeting. The steps do not remove the harmful argument. They give the other argument enough time to be built.

The first two steps are about words, the third is about other people, the fourth is about the clock, the fifth is about a standard you trust, and the last one is about the next small act rather than the whole plan. **Self-control** in this sense is not the absence of feeling. It is the extra two minutes given to the second argument, so that the second argument exists at all.
examples: First the argument for, then the argument against.
Who pays for this decision?
I am too tired to decide this now, so it waits until tomorrow morning.
sections.heading: How to keep the good argument alive
steps: Name the two arguments out loud, one after the other: first the one that supports the act, then the one that stops it.
Write down what the harm argument says, in its best form, as if a sensible person had said it.
Check who pays: name the person who carries the cost, and say whether that person is in the room.
Move the decision to a moment when you are not tired, if the delay costs nothing; if the delay does cost something, decide anyway and write the cost down.
Ask what a person you respect would say about this exact decision, and note the part you would not say out loud.
Make the next small decision the honest one, and let the habit follow the act.

terms.example: A little self-control before the reply is cheaper than a retraction later.
terms.gloss: Holding a decision back for a short time so that the second argument can be made.

sections.body:
This article explains a mechanism. It does not excuse anything. A person who hurts somebody is responsible for the harm, whatever the state of mind was at the time. A **conscience** is the sense that tells you an act would hurt somebody; when it argues in favour of the act, that argument is not a permission, it is the point where you know the other side is there.

It does not diagnose anybody either. Nothing here says that a person is a bully or a deceiver, and nothing here gives you a test for such a label. It does not replace **accountability** either: the answer you owe for an act, to the person who was harmed, to the team, to the law. An inner state is not an answer to anybody.

And it does not replace the law or a good conscience. Most of the harm in this article is ordinary harm — a wrong report, a broken promise, a person treated as a number. The law is there for the cases that no personal check will stop. The rest is your own work.
examples: Explaining the mechanism is not excusing the act.
Whatever the state of mind was, the person is still responsible for the harm.
That is a matter of accountability, and it does not wait for a better mood.
sections.heading: What this article does not do

terms.example: His conscience told him the report would hurt the supplier.
terms.gloss: The sense that tells you an act would hurt somebody.

terms.example: The mistake was hers, and the accountability was hers as well.
terms.gloss: The answer you owe for an act, to the people affected and to the law.

sections.body:
Use these at the moment you have to decide, not afterwards. The first two name the two arguments. The next three find the cost, the company and the delay. The last three hold the decision still and put the act in writing.

None of them needs a dramatic voice. The point is not to impress the room; it is to make the second argument audible while there is still time to hear it.
examples: Two arguments: the one that supports this, and the one that stops it.
Let me hear the objection before I decide.
Who carries the cost of this decision?
I am too tired to make this call now, so it waits until tomorrow.
I am not going to decide this one alone.
Write down what the other side would say, in its best form.
The capacity is not the question here; the aim is.
That is the habit talking, so I will check it once before I act.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

sections.body:
A team, a family or a company also holds both arguments. Any group has an argument that moves it forward and an argument that stops it, and both are made by the same people. The difference from one person is that a group has no pause of its own: nobody inside it is obliged to wait.

So the louder argument wins by default. When nobody checks, the decision of the group is the one that was said last, said loudest, or said by the person with the most to gain. The second argument does not disappear. It goes quiet, and quiet arguments are the ones that get lost.

That is why a group needs somebody whose job is to say the second argument. In some teams the job has a name and in others it does not, but the work is the same: ask the question nobody wants to answer. The person is often unpopular, because the second argument slows the decision down. The person is often right, because the second argument is the one nobody else made.

An **unwritten rule** grows around such a person — do not bring this up again. The rule is not a rule. It is the group silencing the check. The way to keep the check alive is simple: nobody should be the only person who says the second argument. If one person always says it, that person will be stopped. If everybody can, the check survives.
examples: We have one argument for this and one against it. Let me hear the second one.
Who is the person here who says the second argument?
The decision was made by the loudest voice, not by the best reason.
sections.heading: The same idea in a group

terms.example: The unwritten rule was that nobody questioned the schedule.
terms.gloss: A rule that a group follows although nobody has written it down.

item.summary: Good and bad are not two materials inside a person. They are one capacity, used for two aims. After reading this you can name the five parts of an act, separate the capacity from the aim, explain why the same person can help or harm, read the six factors that turn a decision, and run a six-step check before you act at work, at home or in a meeting.
item.title: Angels and Demons Inside One Person: Good and Evil From One Source
